Tensor Cookbook: Mastering Tensors through Diagrams
Beheshteh T. Rakhshan 1,2 , Guillaume Rabusseau 1,2,3 1 Mila & DIRO, 2 Université de Montréal, 3 CIFAR AI Chair

Abstract




Notations

\bm{\mathcal{A}}

General tensor containing
n\geq 0
modes

\bm{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times d_{3}}

A third-order tensor
\bm{\mathcal{A}}
with shape
(d_{1},d_{2},d_{3})

\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{i,j,k}

The
(i,j,k)
’th element of a third-order tensor
\bm{\mathcal{A}}

\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{i,:,k}

Mode-2 fiber of a third-order tensor
\mathbf{\bm{\mathcal{A}}}
, equivalent to a vector
\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}}

\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{(2)}

Mode-2 flattening of a (third-order) tensor
\bm{\mathcal{A}}
, equivalent to a matrix
\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}\times d_{1}d_{3}}

\mathrm{vec}(\bm{\mathcal{A}})

A vector obtained by concatenating mode-
N
fibers of
\bm{\mathcal{A}}
, equivalent to a vector
\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}d_{2}d_{3}}

\bm{\mathcal{A}}\circ\bm{\mathcal{B}}

The tensor product (equiv. outer product) of tensors
\bm{\mathcal{A}}
and
\bm{\mathcal{B}}

\left\langle\bm{\mathcal{A}},\bm{\mathcal{B}}\right\rangle

Inner product between tensors
\bm{\mathcal{A}}
and
\bm{\mathcal{B}}

\left\lVert\bm{\mathcal{A}}\right\rVert_{F}

Frobenius norm of the tensor
\bm{\mathcal{A}}

\bm{\mathcal{A}}\otimes\bm{\mathcal{B}}

The Kronecker product of tensors
\bm{\mathcal{A}}
and
\bm{\mathcal{B}}

\mathbf{A}

A matrix; equivalently, a rank-2 tensor or tensor of order 2

\mathbf{A}_{ij}

The
ij
-th element of the matrix
\mathbf{A}

\mathbf{A}^{-1}

The inverse matrix of matrix
\mathbf{A}

\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{T}}

The transposed matrix of matrix
\mathbf{A}

\mathbf{I}

The identity matrix

\mathbf{A}\odot\mathbf{B}

The Khatri-Rao product of matrices
\mathbf{A}
and
\mathbf{B}

\mathbf{A}*\mathbf{B}

The Hadamard product of matrices
\mathbf{A}
and
\mathbf{B}

\mathbf{a}

Column vector; A rank-1 tensor

\mathbf{a}_{i}

The
i
-th element of vector
\mathbf{a}

a

Scalar; A rank-0 tensor

Tensor Network Notations

-th order tensor
\bm{\mathcal{A}}

Introduction

High–dimensional data arise naturally in many areas of science and engineering, including machine learning, signal processing, computational physics, and statistics. Such data are often represented as tensors, i.e., multi–dimensional generalizations of matrices. While tensors provide a natural representation for multi–modal structure, their direct manipulation quickly becomes challenging as the order of the tensor grows: the number of parameters increases exponentially, and algebraic expressions involving many indices become difficult to interpret and implement.

Tensor networks (TNs) provide an effective framework for addressing these challenges.
Originally introduced by
30
and extensively developed in the quantum physics community, the graphical language of tensor networks encodes tensor contractions as edges in a graph, a formalism that not only reduces notational overhead but also reveals structural properties of tensor operations that are obscured by index notation. Despite the central role of high-dimensional tensors in modern machine learning and numerical analysis, tensor network diagrams remain underutilized outside of quantum computing, partly due to the lack of a self-contained mathematical reference accessible to a broad technical audience.
The goal of this manuscript is to provide a self-contained guide to tensor networks and their use in tensor algebra. We present the main operations on tensors, such as contractions, products, and reshaping, through graphical notation, and show how classical tensor decompositions and related computations can be naturally expressed in this framework. In addition, we illustrate how tensor networks simplify the derivation of gradients and the manipulation of high-dimensional probability distributions.

Throughout, we demonstrate that the diagrammatic approach does not merely simplify notation; it yields genuinely shorter and more transparent proofs of classical identities, rank bounds, and gradient formulas that would otherwise require laborious index manipulation.

Organization

This manuscript is organized into five chapters, each building on the previous to develop
a complete and self-contained treatment of tensor networks.

Chapter 1: Tensor Network Basics.

We introduce the graphical language of tensor networks from first principles. Tensors are
represented as nodes with labeled legs, and contractions are encoded as shared edges. We
develop the core operations: inner products, outer products, traces, and Frobenius norms within this framework, demonstrating how familiar matrix identities extend naturally to
higher-order tensors. The chapter concludes with copy tensors (hyperedges) and graphical
representations of matrix factorizations, including QR decomposition and singular value
decomposition (SVD).

Chapter 2: Operations on Tensors.

We treat tensor reshaping operations, fibers, slices, matricization, and vectorization, formally and graphically. We then develop the principal tensor products: the mode-
n

product, the Kronecker product, the Khatri-Rao product, and the Hadamard product, each accompanied by diagrammatic proofs of their key identities. The chapter closes with a general theorem bounding the rank of tensor matricizations via cuts in the tensor network graph, unifying several classical rank inequalities under a single framework.

Chapter 3: Tensor Decompositions.

We present the three principal decomposition models for high-dimensional tensors. The CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) decomposition expresses a tensor as a sum of rank-one terms; the Tucker decomposition generalizes this via a compressed core tensor and factor matrices,
and the Tensor Train (TT) decomposition provides a chain-structured factorization whose parameter count scales linearly with tensor order. For each model, we provide the mathematical formulation, its tensor network diagram, rank characterizations, and computational algorithms, including Higher-Order SVD (HOSVD) for Tucker and the TT-SVD and Alternating Least Squares (ALS) algorithms for TT. We further discuss efficient algebraic operations in TT format and briefly survey advanced architectures, including Tensor Ring, Projected Entangled Pair States (PEPS), and Hierarchical Tucker decompositions.

Chapter 4: Computing Gradients of Tensor Networks.

We develop a graphical calculus for the differentiation of tensor network functions. Starting
from classical definitions of gradients and Jacobians, we establish that the Jacobian of a tensor network with respect to any core tensor is obtained simply by removing that core from the diagram. This yields transparent, diagram-level proofs of classical derivative
identities, including gradients of quadratic forms and trace functionals, and extends naturally to networks where a core appears multiple times. We illustrate the framework with two applications: gradient-based optimization of
the CP decomposition, and backpropagation through weight matrices parameterized in
Matrix Product Operator (MPO) format.

Chapter 5: Probability Distributions and Random Tensor Networks.

We explore two interconnected applications of tensor networks to probability and
statistics. First, we show how joint probability distributions over discrete random
variables can be encoded as tensors, and how marginals and conditionals reduce to simple
diagrammatic operations. We then discuss how the Tensor Train format provides an
efficient, structured parameterization of high-dimensional distributions, including
Born Machine-style representations rooted in quantum physics. Second, we compute
the expectations of random tensor networks whose entries are drawn from the standard normal
distribution. Using Isserlis’ theorem and diagrammatic reasoning, we derive closed-form
expressions for quantities such as
\mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\|_{F}^{2}]
and

\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{A})^{\otimes 2}]
with a brevity that would be difficult to achieve through conventional index-based methods.

Target Audience

This manuscript is intended as a self-contained reference for researchers and
practitioners who work with high-dimensional data and wish to develop fluency with tensor
networks. The material is broadly accessible: a working knowledge of linear algebra
at the level of a first undergraduate course, including matrix multiplication,
QR decomposition, and SVD are sufficient for the majority of the text.

The presentation is designed to serve multiple communities simultaneously. For

mathematicians
, the manuscript provides rigorous
definitions, rank characterizations, and algorithm analyses grounded in linear algebra
theory. For
researchers in machine learning and data science
, it offers a practical
toolkit to parameterize high-dimensional weight matrices, compute gradients through
structured tensor decompositions, and compactly model complex distributions. For

physicists and quantum computing researchers
, it bridges the diagrammatic
conventions of tensor networks with the language of applied mathematics.

All tensor network diagrams in this manuscript are typeset using
L
a
T
e
X
with the
TikZ

package, and the diagrammatic notation is gradually introduced so that no prior exposure
to tensor network diagrams is assumed.

1
Tensor Networks Basics

As their order increases, representing and working with tensors becomes more complicated.
Tensor networks provide an efficient framework for working with these high-order objects, simplifying both their representation and analysis.
The graphical notation of tensor networks offers an intuitive way to visualize and simplify complex tensor operations
[
28
,
3
]
.
In this section, we introduce basic notions on tensors and common tensor operations using the language of tensor networks.

1.1
What are Tensor Networks?

As their name suggests, Tensor Networks (TNs) are simply tensors connected to each other to form a network. More precisely, a tensor network is a graph in which vertices represent
tensors
and edges represent
contracted
indices (shared modes). The graphical notation for tensor networks was first introduced by
30
. Tensors are represented by shapes with legs (edges), i.e.,

We will use different shapes, such as rectangles, triangles, or circles, and various colors to represent tensors. Shapes and colors serve mainly as visual cues.
The
order
of a tensor is its number of dimensions, e.g., an
N
-th order tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
is a multidimensional array of scalars
\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{i_{1},\dots,i_{N}}
indexed by
N
indices
i_{1}\in[d_{1}],i_{2}\in[d_{2}],\cdots,i_{N}\in[d_{N}]
. Each axis is called a
mode
of a tensor: an
N
-th order tensor has
N
modes.

Tensors naturally generalize vectors and matrices to higher-order arrays. As the order increases, representing these arrays becomes more challenging.
Tensor networks
provide a simple and intuitive way to represent and manipulate these higher-order objects. Complex operations on tensors can be represented more easily with graphical notations of tensor networks
[
3
,
28
]
.

Tensor Network Nodes

In a tensor network, each node (or vertex) represents a tensor, and the number of legs (incident edges) corresponds to the order of the tensor: scalars are nodes with no edges, vector nodes have a single edge, matrix nodes have two edges, and so on. For example,

a

\in\mathbb{R}
,

\mathbf{a}

d

\in\mathbb{R}^{d}
,

\mathbf{A}

d_{2}

d_{1}

\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}}
,

\bm{\mathcal{A}}

d_{2}

d_{1}

d_{3}

\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times d_{3}}
,

d_{2}

d_{1}

d_{3}

d_{4}

\bm{\mathcal{B}}

\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times d_{3}\times d_{4}}
.

represent a scalar, a vector, a matrix, a third- and a fourth-order tensors, respectively.
Throughout this manuscript,

•

Tensors are represented by colored shapes called nodes, where the colors and shapes have no specific meaning (unless stated otherwise).

•

We use lower case letters for scalars (e.g.,
a
), bold lower case letters for vectors (e.g.,
\mathbf{v}
), bold upper case letters for matrices (e.g.,
\mathbf{M}
), and
bold upper case calligraphic letters for higher-order tensors (e.g.,
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
).

•

The dimension of each mode of a tensor is depicted by a gray letter positioned at the top of the corresponding leg, e.g.,

Tensor Network Edges

In tensor network diagram, legs are of two types: contracted legs (those connecting two tensors) and un-contracted legs, also called free legs, with one dangling end (i.e., a leg that is not connected to any other tensor). As mentioned above, un-contracted legs correspond to free indices: the number of free legs indicates the order of a tensor: scalars have no free legs, vectors have one, matrices have two, and higher-order tensors have three or more. Contracted legs represent contractions:
tensors can be connected along legs of the same size, which represents a summation (contraction) over the connected modes.
We use the terms summation and contraction interchangeably. The most common contraction operation is
matrix multiplication
. For two matrices
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times R},\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d_{2}}
, their matrix product corresponds to a contraction between the second mode of
\mathbf{A}
and the first mode of
\mathbf{B}
:

From mathematical expressions to tensor networks, and back

Tensor networks are simple to work with because there are no strict rules for representing legs and nodes.
In tensor network diagrams, nodes and edges can be positioned arbitrarily in the plane, only the graph structure matters.
For example, when translating matrix multiplication into a tensor network diagram, the key feature is to ensure the dimension of the connected legs are consistent, e.g., for
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times R},\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d_{2}}
all diagrams below illustrate the
same
matrix multiplication:

Note that because of the sizes of
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times R}
and
\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d_{2}}
, there is only one way to do the contraction between the two; hence, there would be no ambiguity in the diagrams above even if we omitted the dimensions on the edges.

Conversely, translating tensor network diagrams into mathematical formulations can lead to multiple interpretations. For example, the following matrix multiplication diagram

\mathbf{A}

\mathbf{B}

R

d_{1}

d_{2}

can be interpreted differently depending on what we choose the shapes of
\mathbf{A}
,
\mathbf{B}
and the resulting matrix to be:

•

if
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times R},\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d_{2}}
and the result is of size
d_{1}\times d_{2}
, then the diagram represents the product
\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}
,

•

if
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d_{1}},\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d_{2}}
and the result is of size
d_{1}\times d_{2}
, then the diagram represents the product
\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{B}
,

•

if
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d_{1}},\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d_{2}}
and the result is of size
d_{2}\times d_{1}
, then the diagram represents the product
\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{A}
,

•

…

Therefore, one should be mindful when translating tensor network diagrams into mathematical formulations. But this is also what makes tensor networks very useful! When we are working with the diagrams, rather than mathematical expressions, we do not need to care about, e.g., transposes.

Contracting two legs of the same node.

As explained previously, any two legs of the same dimension can be connected to form an edge in a tensor network, even two legs corresponding to the same node. Consider for example a fifth-order tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times d_{3}\times d_{2}\times d_{4}}
. Since its 2nd and 4th modes have the same dimension, we can contract them together. Since the resulting tensor network has 3 dangling legs, it represents a third-order tensor:

When contracting two legs of an
N
-th order tensor, the resulting tensor is of order
N-2
. This is closely related to the notion of
partial trace
that we will present later.

1.2
Inner Product, Outer Product, Trace and Norm

In this section, we use tensor networks to show how the classical notions of inner product, outer product, trace, and norm can be generalized to higher-order tensors.

Inner product

Similarly to the classical inner (Euclidean) product between vectors, the inner product of two
N
-th order tensors
\bm{\mathcal{S}},\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\dots\times d_{N}}
is the sum of the products of their entries:

\langle\bm{\mathcal{S}},\bm{\mathcal{T}}\rangle=\sum_{i_{1}=1}^{d_{1}}\dots\sum_{i_{N}=1}^{d_{N}}\bm{\mathcal{S}}_{i_{1}\dots i_{N}}\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{i_{1}\dots i_{N}}.

In a tensor network diagram, the summation over all dimensions is obtained by connecting all the legs of the two tensors. This results in a tensor network without free legs, representing a scalar. For example, for vectors
\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times 1},\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times 1}
we have

\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{b}_{i}=\hbox to53.89pt{\vbox to27.1pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 12.50961pt\lower-12.92343pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}
{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} {}\lxSVG@fillstroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 16.76 0 C 16.76 9.25 9.25 16.76 0 16.76 C -9.25 16.76 -16.76 9.25 -16.76 0 C -16.76 -9.25 -9.25 -16.76 0 -16.76 C 9.25 -16.76 16.76 -9.25 16.76 0 Z M 0 0}{} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope }{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-11.68402pt}{-3.22221pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}

In this book, we will focus only on real-valued tensors, but the tensor network formalism can easily be adapted to complex-valued ones.
For example, if the two tensors were complex-valued, one would have to take the conjugates of the entries of the second tensor, which could be indicated in the tensor network by having node
\bm{\mathcal{T}}^{*}
(component-wise conjugate) instead of
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
.

Outer product

Recall that the outer product of two vectors
\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{m},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
is the
m\times n
rank-one matrix
\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^{\top}
.
This operation can be generalized to any number of tensors. For example, the outer product of
N
vectors,
\mathbf{a}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}},\cdots,\mathbf{a}_{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{N}}
, is the tensor of order
N
defined by

\displaystyle(\mathbf{a}_{1}\circ\mathbf{a}_{2}\circ\cdots\circ\mathbf{a}_{N})_{i_{1},i_{2},\cdots,i_{n}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\hskip-28.45274pt(\mathbf{a}_{1})_{i_{1}}(\mathbf{a}_{2})_{i_{2}}\cdots(\mathbf{a}_{N})_{i_{N}}\ \text{for all }i_{1}\in[d_{1}],\cdots,i_{N}\in[d_{N}].

Such a tensor is called a
rank-one
tensor. The diagram below illustrates the outer product of
N
vectors:

\mathbf{a}_{1}\circ\mathbf{a}_{2}\circ\cdots\circ\mathbf{a}_{N}=\hbox to122.67pt{\vbox to29.15pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 29.70387pt\lower-21.31703pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

As a special case, for
N=2
, we have
\mathbf{a}_{1}\circ\mathbf{a}_{2}=\mathbf{a}_{1}\mathbf{a}_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}}
. As we see in the tensor network diagram of the outer product, there are no shared edges, which indeed reflects that no contraction (summation) occurs in an outer product.
The notion of an outer product can naturally be extended to higher-order tensors.
Let
\bm{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{1}\times\dots\times m_{p}}
and
\bm{\mathcal{B}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times\dots\times n_{q}}
. The outer product of
\bm{\mathcal{A}}
and
\bm{\mathcal{B}}
is the tensor of order
p+q
defined by

(\bm{\mathcal{A}}\circ\bm{\mathcal{B}})_{i_{1},i_{2},\cdots,i_{p},j_{1},j_{2},\cdots,j_{q}}=\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{i_{1},i_{2},\cdots,i_{p}}\bm{\mathcal{B}}_{j_{1},j_{2},\cdots,j_{q}}.

Like for vectors, the tensor networks of the outer product is simply obtained by juxtaposing the corresponding nodes without adding any edge:

\bm{\mathcal{A}}\circ\bm{\mathcal{B}}=\hbox to61.63pt{\vbox to37.38pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip-139.93513pt\lower-20.84258pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

and

.

In the proposition below we show a simple visual proof of the fact that inner products of outer products are products of inner products.

Proposition 1
.

Let
\bm{\mathcal{X}},\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
with
\bm{\mathcal{X}}=\mathbf{a}_{1}\circ\mathbf{a}_{2}\circ\cdots\circ\mathbf{a}_{N}
and
\bm{\mathcal{T}}=\mathbf{t}_{1}\circ\mathbf{t}_{2}\circ\cdots\circ\mathbf{t}_{N}
, then
\langle\bm{\mathcal{X}},\bm{\mathcal{T}}\rangle=\prod_{n=1}^{N}\langle\mathbf{a}_{n},\mathbf{t}_{n}\rangle

Edge of dimension one = no edge

Note that in tensor network diagrams, an edge of size one is equivalent to having no edge.
For example, in the matrix multiplication, if the contraction edge is of size one, it is equivalent to the outer product of vectors:

Trace

The trace operation is a special case of tensor contraction applied on square matrices. In tensor networks, the trace is naturally represented by a loop (self-edge) connecting the two legs of the matrix:

and
\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d}
. As we explained before, when drawing the graph of a tensor network, only the graph structure is important. This allows us to see that

Note that the equalities between the tensor network diagrams are trivial: we just changed the nodes’ position without changing the underlying graph’s structure. We thus simply interpreted the same diagram in two ways, leading to a less trivial equality between
\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{C})
and
\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})
.

Partial traces

The
partial trace
is a common operation used in particular in the context of modeling many-body quantum systems, where density matrices of a part of a system are obtained by performing a partial trace of the density matrix of the whole system. Without delving into the specifics of quantum systems, consider a square matrix of dimension
d_{1}d_{2}\times d_{1}d_{2}
which we interpret as a fourth-order tensor

d_{1}

d_{2}

d_{1}

d_{2}

\bm{\mathcal{T}}
.
The partial trace of
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
over the subspace
\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}}
is the
d_{2}\times d_{2}
matrix obtained by “tracing out” the
d_{1}
dimension by connecting the corresponding legs:

d_{2}

d_{2}

d_{1}

\bm{\mathcal{T}}
. Similarly, the partial trace of
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
over the subspace
\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}}
is the
d_{1}\times d_{1}
matrix

d_{1}

d_{1}

d_{2}

\bm{\mathcal{T}}
.

Tensor Frobenius Norm

The Frobenius norm of a tensor
\bm{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
is the square root of the sum of its
squared elements (i.e., the square root of the inner product with itself). In tensor networks, the norm of a third-order tensor
\bm{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times d_{3}}
is represented as

\displaystyle\left\lVert\bm{\mathcal{A}}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=\langle\bm{\mathcal{A}},\bm{\mathcal{A}}\rangle=\sum_{i_{1}=1}^{d_{1}}\sum_{i_{2}=1}^{d_{2}}\sum_{i_{3}=1}^{d_{3}}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{i_{1}i_{2}i_{3}}^{2}=\hbox to55.35pt{\vbox to46.41pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 13.44638pt\lower-21.7816pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

\lxSVG@closescope }{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-12.63892pt}{-3.41666pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}

Frobenius norm of outer products

Using tensor networks, it is almost trivial to show that the Frobenius norm of an outer product is equal to the product of the Frobenius norms. E.g., for
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}
and
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times d_{3}}
, we have

1.3
Copy Tensors (Hyperedges)

Sometimes, one needs to represent a simultaneous contraction shared among more than two tensors. Consider, for example, the following contraction between three vectors,
\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},
and
\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}
to obtain a scalar:
\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{b}_{i}\mathbf{c}_{i}
.
This operation can be depicted in tensor networks using a special tensor called
copy tensor
. The copy tensor is equivalent to a Kronecker delta, i.e., a hyper-diagonal tensor with ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere, and is represented as a black dot in tensor network diagrams. E.g., the copy tensor

is defined element-wise as

3.

tensor (obtained by merging the contracted legs and dots in the tensor network diagram). For example:

1.4
Matrix Factorization in Tensor Networks

Tensor factorizations can be depicted in tensor network diagrams, just like any other operation. In this section, we will introduce graphical diagrams for matrix factorizations. More general factorizations of higher-order tensors will be covered in Chapter
3
. In tensor networks, factorization means splitting a single node into multiple nodes. We will refer to its inverse operation as merging, i.e., combining multiple nodes into a single node. This process can be clearly illustrated in the following tensor network diagram:

\mathbf{A}

\mathbf{B}

\mathbf{C}

\mathbf{D}

r_{1}

r_{2}

r_{3}

r_{3}

d_{1}

d_{2}

\xrightarrow{\text{merging}}

\xleftarrow[\text{factorizing}]{}

\mathbf{M}

d_{2}

d_{1}

Therefore, we can represent any matrix decomposition in tensor network diagrams. We will see in the following chapters that the QR and singular value decompositions (SVD) are two decompositions that are often used in tensor network algorithm to split nodes. Both of these decompositions factorize a matrix into a product of matrices, some of them satisfying orthogonality constraints. We will use visual cues to represent such orthogonality constraints in tensor network diagrams:

Left and right orthonormal matrices and tensors

We call a matrix
\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}

left-orthogonal
if the contraction of its transpose with itself from the left yields the identity matrix (
\mathbf{U}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{I}_{n}
).
Similarly, a matrix
\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}
is
right-orthogonal
if the contraction with its transpose from the right yields the identity matrix
(
\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}=\mathbf{I}_{m}
). In tensor network diagrams, we will use half-colored nodes to denote such orthogonality structure, in such a way that when connecting two copies of an orthogonal node using the legs on the uncolored part, the result is the identity. For example, a left orthogonal matrix
\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}
will be represented as

\mathbf{U}

m

n

, leading to

\mathbf{U}
\mathbf{U}

m

n

n

=

n

=

\mathbf{I}_{n}
.
Similarly, a right-orthogonal matrix
\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}
will be drawn as

\mathbf{V}

m

n

and we have

\mathbf{V}
\mathbf{V}

n

m

m

=

=

m

\mathbf{I}_{m}
.

Note that if the matrix
\mathbf{U}
is left orthogonal then
\mathbf{U}\mathbf{U}^{\mathsf{T}}
is not necessarily the identity, i.e.,

is given by

2
Operations on Tensors

Recall that a tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
can be seen as a multi-dimensional array of order
N
: an
N
-th order or
N
-way tensor has
N
modes, each mode corresponding to one dimension
[
20
]
.

Tensor Fibers

For any mode-
i
(where
i=1,\dots,N
), tensor
fibers
are obtained by keeping all indices fixed except the
i
-th one. For example, a matrix column corresponds to a mode-1 fiber, while a matrix row corresponds to a mode-2 fiber. In a third-order tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times d_{3}}
, we have
d_{2}d_{3}
mode-1 fibers, which are vectors of size
d_{1}
, i.e.,
\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{:,i_{2},i_{3}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}}
for
i_{2}\in[d_{2}]
and
i_{3}\in[d_{3}]
. The colon indicates varying the first index, while
i_{2}
and
i_{3}
remain fixed. Fibers are vectors.

Tensor Slices

Slices of a tensor are two-dimensional arrays (matrices) obtained by fixing all but two indices. For a third-order tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times d_{3}}
, there are horizontal, lateral, and frontal slices denoted by
\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{i_{1},:,:}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}\times d_{3}}
,
\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{:,i_{2},:}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{3}}
, and
\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{:,:,i_{3}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}}
, respectively. Therefore, slices are matrices.

Scalar Multiplication

Let
\lambda\in\mathbb{R}
be a scalar. The scalar product
\lambda\bm{\mathcal{T}}

is a tensor of the same dimension
d_{1}\times\cdots\times d_{N}
, defined element-wise by:

(\lambda\bm{\mathcal{T}})_{i_{1}\cdots i_{N}}=\lambda\cdot\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{i_{1}\cdots i_{N}}

for all admissible indices
i_{k}\in[d_{k}]
and
k\in[N]
.

Tensors Sum

Let
\bm{\mathcal{S}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
. The sum of tensors
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
and
\bm{\mathcal{S}}
is a tensor of the same dimension,
\bm{\mathcal{T}}+\bm{\mathcal{S}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
, defined element-wise by:
(\bm{\mathcal{T}}+\bm{\mathcal{S}})_{i_{1},\cdots,i_{N}}=\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{i_{1},\cdots,i_{N}}+\bm{\mathcal{S}}_{i_{1},\cdots,i_{N}}
for all admissible indices
i_{k}\in[d_{k}]
and
k\in[N]
.

2.1
Permute and Reshape Tensors

Permutation and reshaping are two fundamental operations on tensors.

•

Permutation
rearranges the indices of a tensor without changing its number of modes. A common example of a permutation is the transpose of a matrix.

•

Reshaping
combines multiple indices into larger ones or divides a large index into multiple smaller indices, reducing or increasing the total number of indices while preserving the overall size of the tensor.

We introduce matricization and vectorization, two common reshaping operations on tensors.

Definition 2
.

(Matricization)
Let
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
. The mode-
n
matricization
\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{(n)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{n}\times d_{1}d_{2}\cdots d_{n-1}d_{n+1}\cdots d_{N}}
, for
n\in[N]
, is obtained by unfolding
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
into a matrix by taking all mode-
n
fibers and stacking them as columns. For example, the matricization of a tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times d_{3}}
along mode-
1
, which is denoted by
\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{(1)}
, is the
d_{1}\times d_{2}d_{3}
matrix

\begin{bmatrix}\vline&\vline&\vline&\vline\\
\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{:,1,1}&{\bm{\mathcal{T}}}_{:,1,2}&\dots&{\bm{\mathcal{T}}}_{:,d_{2},d_{3}}\\
\vline&\vline&\vline&\vline\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}d_{3}}.

The mode-2 and mode-3 matricizations
\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{(2)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}\times d_{1}d_{3}}
and
\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{(3)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{3}\times d_{1}d_{2}}
are defined similarly.

Observe that in mode-1 matricization, the two indices corresponding to the second and third modes of
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
are grouped together to form a new index that ranges from 1 to
d_{2}d_{3}
. In the previous definition, we chose to order this new index using lexicographic ordering, e.g.,
11,12,13,21,22,23,31,32,33
if
d_{2}=d_{3}=3
. Different orderings of the columns for matricizations are sometimes used (e.g., reverse lexicographic in
[
20
]
). In general, the specific ordering
used is not important, but it must be consistent across related calculations (see
[
21
]
for further details).

\displaystyle=(\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{(\{1,2,6\})})_{i_{1}i_{2}i_{6},i_{3}i_{4}i_{5}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}d_{2}d_{6}\times d_{3}d_{4}d_{5}}.

While this concept is intuitive, it is clunky to write formally: the indices
i_{r_{1}},i_{r_{2}},\cdots,i_{r_{|I|}}
in
I
(decreasingly ordered) of a tensor are mapped to the row index
j=1+\sum_{l=1}^{|I|}\left[(i_{r_{l}}-1)\prod_{m=1}^{l-1}I_{r_{m}}\right]
, while the remaining indices
i_{c_{1}},i_{c_{2}},\cdots,i_{c_{N-|I|}}
(again decreasingly ordered) are mapped to the column index
k=1+\sum_{n=1}^{N-|I|}\left[(i_{c_{n}}-1)\prod_{s=1}^{n-1}I_{r_{s}}\right]
. Using tensor networks allows us to abstract away this clunkiness by simply representing such
reshaping operations by grouping legs together.

Likewise, just as a tensor can be converted into a matrix, it can also be converted into a vector. This process is called vectorization:

Definition 3
.

(Vectorization)
Let
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
. The
vectorization
of
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
denoted as
\mathrm{vec}(\bm{\mathcal{T}})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}d_{2}\cdots d_{N}}
is the vector obtained by concatenating its mode-
N
fibers
1
1

1

Using the lexicographic order.
. For example, the vectorization of a tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times d_{3}}
is given by:

Vectorization is a flattening operation that converts a tensor of any order into a vector. Similarly to matricization, in tensor networks
the edge of the shape

d_{1}

d_{2}

d_{3}

represents an edge of size
d_{1}d_{2}d_{3}
. In general, throughout this manuscript, convergent edges represent an edge whose size is the product of the sizes of all associated edges. Note that the vectorization of a tensor is equal to the vectorization
2
2

2

To be consistent with the definition of vectorization used in this book, the vectorization of a matrix is given by the concatenation of its rows, which is sometimes referred to as
row-major vectorization
.Note that this is the default vectorizing operation,
ravel()
, of the
numpy
package in
Python
.
of the mode-
1
matricization of the tensor, i.e., for
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\cdots\times d_{N}}
,
\mathrm{vec}(\bm{\mathcal{T}})=\mathrm{vec}(\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{(1)})
.

2.2
Products

Tensors can be combined or
multiplied
using different types of operation. In this section, we provide graphical illustrations of different product operations.

Mode-
n
Tensor Product

The modes
n
products, where a tensor is multiplied by a matrix along a specific mode, can be seen as a generalization of the matrix products. More precisely, the mode-
n
product generalizes matrix-matrix multiplication along one particular mode. These include mode-
n
products between tensors and matrices, as well as tensors and vectors.

1.

Mode-n product (matrix).

The mode-
n
product of a tensor
\bm{\mathcal{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
with a matrix
\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{n}}
denoted as

\bm{\mathcal{X}}\times_{n}\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\cdots\times d_{n-1}\times m\times d_{n+1}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
is defined as the contraction of a tensor with a matrix along mode-
n
of the tensor and mode-2 of the matrix (column index), i.e.,

However, if

(\bm{\mathcal{X}}\times_{n}\mathbf{B})\times_{n}\mathbf{A}
is not valid unless
n=d_{n}=p
.

We show in the following proposition how the mode-
n
product can be expressed through matricization and matrix product.

Proposition 3
.

Let
\bm{\mathcal{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\dots\times d_{N}}
and
\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{n}}
then

(\bm{\mathcal{X}}\times_{n}\mathbf{M})_{(n)}=\mathbf{M}\bm{\mathcal{X}}_{(n)}
.

Proof.

n=2
and
N=3
. The extension to the general case is straightforward. We have

2.

Mode-n product (vector).
The mode-
n
product of a tensor
\bm{\mathcal{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
with a vector
\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{n}}
, is denoted by

\bm{\mathcal{X}}\times_{n}\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\cdots\times d_{n-1}\times d_{n+1}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
. Note that the result is a tensor of order
N-1
. It can be pictured in a tensor network diagram as

\bm{\mathcal{X}}\times_{n}\mathbf{v}=\hbox to62.89pt{\vbox to53.07pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip-139.0773pt\lower-37.38866pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

Note that in mode-
n
vector multiplication, unlike mode-
n
matrix multiplication, the order of multiplication matters as a vector contraction reduces the tensor order by 1, so subsequent mode indices shift. Let
\bm{\mathcal{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\cdots\times d_{m}\times\cdots\times d_{n}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
and
\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{n}},\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{m}}
, then

\bm{\mathcal{X}}\times_{n}\mathbf{a}\times_{m}\mathbf{b}\neq(\bm{\mathcal{X}}\times_{m}\mathbf{b})\times_{n}\mathbf{a},

as mode-
n
vector multiplication drops the
m
-th dimension
[
1
]
.

Next, we introduce several important products that are often used in tensor derivations: Kronecker, Khatri-Rao, and Hadamard products.

Kronecker product

Let
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}
and
\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}
. The Kronecker product,
\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{mp\times nq}
is defined by

\displaystyle\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}=\begin{bmatrix}a_{11}\mathbf{B}&a_{12}\mathbf{B}&\dots&a_{1n}\mathbf{B}\\
a_{21}\mathbf{B}&a_{22}\mathbf{B}&\dots&a_{2n}\mathbf{B}\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
a_{m1}\mathbf{B}&a_{m2}\mathbf{B}&\dots&a_{mn}\mathbf{B}\end{bmatrix}.

(9)

As one can see from this diagram, the Kronecker product of two matrices is nothing else than a reshaping of their outer products. Indeed, it is easy to convince oneself that every component
a_{i,j}b_{k,l}
of the outer product
\mathbf{A}\circ\mathbf{B}
is present in
\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}
; while the outer product is a fourth-order tensor, the Kronecker product is one of its matricizations. One could show more precisely that
\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}=(\mathbf{A}\circ\mathbf{B})_{(\{1,3\})}
, but we will refrain from doing so and trust the simpler and direct view given by tensor network diagrams: grouping the row legs of
\mathbf{A}
and
\mathbf{B}
on one side, and their column legs on the other, we obtain the matrix called the Kronecker product of
\mathbf{A}
and
\mathbf{B}
:

Remark 4
.

In the following, we list some useful properties of the Kronecker product.

1.

The Kronecker product is not commutative, i.e.,
\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}\neq\mathbf{B}\otimes\mathbf{A}
in general.

2.

\mathbf{I}\otimes\mathbf{A}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{A}&0&\dots&0\\
0&\mathbf{A}&\dots&0\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
0&0&\dots&\mathbf{A}\end{bmatrix}

is a block diagonal matrix.

3.

The Kronecker product of two tensors of the same order results in a tensor of the same order, while their outer product produces a tensor with double the order.

4.

By reshaping the Kronecker product
\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}
, the outer product
\mathbf{A}\circ\mathbf{B}
can be obtained.

5.

The Kronecker product of two identity matrices is a larger identity matrix, i.e.,
\mathbf{I}_{m}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{n}=\mathbf{I}_{mn}
, which can easily be seen by drawing the tensor network diagram:

\hbox to98.6pt{\vbox to34.09pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 17.21292pt\lower-15.62395pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}
{}{{}}{}{{}}
{}{}
{}{}

7.

The Kronecker product satisfies the so-called mixed product property:
(\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B})(\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{D})=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{C}\otimes\mathbf{B}\mathbf{D}
where
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q},\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}
and
\mathbf{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times k}
.

and vice versa when dealing with identities involving Kronecker products.

10.

The
Sylvester Identity
is a very useful identity connecting vectorization, matrix product, and Kronecker product:

\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{B})=(\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}})\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{X}),

where
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}
and
\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}.

Proof.

The proof is rather direct using tensor networks:

It is easy in the last diagram to identify the vectorization of
\mathbf{X}
and the Kronecker product of
\mathbf{A}
and
\mathbf{B}
, and thus to conclude that this tensor network represents a matrix-vector product between the two. However, when translating the tensor network in classical mathematical notation, some care is required. First, we can see that since
\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{X})
is of dimension
np
, the Kronecker product has to be between
\mathbf{A}
and
\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}}
to obtain a matrix of shape
mq\times np
. Then, we need to know which Kronecker product to use:
\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}}
or
\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}}\otimes\mathbf{A}
, which are both of the correct shape. Because in this manuscript we use lexicographic ordering for reshape operations such as
\mathrm{vec}
, the correct formulation is
\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}}
. However, if we were to use reverse lexicographic ordering, as in
[
20
]
, the correct formulation would be
\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}}\otimes\mathbf{A}
.
∎

The
Sylvester identity
is a useful identity to solve systems of equations of the form
\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{X}\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{C}
.

There are useful relationships between the
n
-mode product, matricization, and Kronecker products:

Proposition 5
.

Let
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times\dots\times d_{p}}
,
\mathbf{A}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times n_{1}},\mathbf{A}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}\times n_{2}},\dots,

\mathbf{A}_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{p}\times n_{p}}
, then

\displaystyle(\bm{\mathcal{T}}\times_{1}\mathbf{A}_{1}\times_{2}\mathbf{A}_{2}\times_{3}\mathbf{A}_{3}\times_{4}\dots\times_{p}\mathbf{A}_{p})_{(n)}=\mathbf{A}_{n}\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{(n)}(\mathbf{A}_{1}\otimes\dots\otimes\mathbf{A}_{n-1}\otimes\mathbf{A}_{n+1}\otimes\dots\otimes\mathbf{A}_{p})^{\mathsf{T}}.

Proof.

For
p=3
and
n=1
,

\displaystyle(\bm{\mathcal{T}}\times_{1}\mathbf{A}_{1}\times_{2}\mathbf{A}_{2}\times_{3}\mathbf{A}_{3})_{(1)}

\displaystyle=\left(\hbox to117.78pt{\vbox to67.62pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip-111.82916pt\lower-51.9378pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}
{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} {}\lxSVG@fillstroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 246.98 -41.34 C 246.98 -35.4 242.16 -30.58 236.22 -30.58 C 230.28 -30.58 225.46 -35.4 225.46 -41.34 C 225.46 -47.28 230.28 -52.1 236.22 -52.1 C 242.16 -52.1 246.98 -47.28 246.98 -41.34 Z M 236.22 -41.34}{} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

∎

Proposition 6
.

Let
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times\cdots\times d_{p}}
and
\mathbf{A}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}\times n_{i}}
for
i\in[p]
. Let
m\in[p]
and

\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{([m])}
denotes reshaping the tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
in a matrix of size
d_{1}d_{2}\cdots d_{m}\times d_{m+1}...d_{p}
by mapping the first
m
indices to
rows and the remaining ones to columns. Then,

\displaystyle(\bm{\mathcal{T}}\times_{1}\mathbf{A}_{1}\times_{2}\mathbf{A}_{2}\cdots\times_{p}\mathbf{A}_{p})_{([m])}=(\mathbf{A}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{A}_{2}\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathbf{A}_{m})\mathbf{T}_{([m])}(\mathbf{A}_{m+1}\otimes\mathbf{A}_{m+2}\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathbf{A}_{p})^{\mathsf{T}}.

This identity can be extended to arbitrary subsets
I\subset[p]
:

(\bm{\mathcal{T}}\times_{1}\mathbf{A}_{1}\times_{2}\mathbf{A}_{2}\cdots\times_{p}\mathbf{A}_{p})_{(I)}=\left(\bigotimes_{i\in I}\mathbf{A}_{i}\right)\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{([m])}\left(\bigotimes_{i\in[p]\setminus I}\mathbf{A}_{i}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}.

Khatri-Rao product

The Khatri-Rao product is the column-wise Kronecker product
[
31
,
4
]
. Let
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times R}
and
\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times R}
. The Khatri-Rao product of
\mathbf{A}
and
\mathbf{B}
, denoted as
\mathbf{A}\odot\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{mn\times R}
, is defined by

\displaystyle\mathbf{A}\odot\mathbf{B}=\begin{bmatrix}\vline&\vline&&\vline\\
\mathbf{a}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{b}_{1}&\mathbf{a}_{2}\otimes\mathbf{b}_{2}&\dots&\mathbf{a}_{R}\otimes\mathbf{b}_{R}\\
\vline&\vline&&\vline\end{bmatrix}=\hbox to49.42pt{\vbox to76.85pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 13.45665pt\lower-42.13225pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

where
\mathbf{a}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{a}_{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}
are the columns of
\mathbf{A}
and
\mathbf{b}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{b}_{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
are the columns of
\mathbf{B}
. In the corresponding tensor network diagram, the copy tensor enforces that the resulting matrix only contains the Kronecker product of
matching
columns of
\mathbf{A}
and
\mathbf{B}
.

Remark 7
.

Some of the Khatri-Rao product properties are listed below:

1.

Like the Kronecker product, the Khatri-Rao product is not commutative, i.e.,
\mathbf{A}\odot\mathbf{B}\neq\mathbf{B}\odot\mathbf{A}
in general.

2.

The Khatri-Rao product is associative, i.e.,
\mathbf{A}\odot(\mathbf{B}\odot\mathbf{C})=(\mathbf{A}\odot\mathbf{B})\odot\mathbf{C}
, where
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times R},\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times R}
and
\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{s\times R}
.

3.

The columns of
\mathbf{A}\odot\mathbf{B}
form a subset of the columns of the Kronecker product
\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}
.

Hadamard product

Let
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}
and
\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}
be matrices of the same shape. The Hadamard (or component-wise) product of
\mathbf{A}
and
\mathbf{B}
is the matrix
\mathbf{A}*\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}
defined element-wise by

(\mathbf{A}*\mathbf{B})_{ij}=\mathbf{A}_{ij}\mathbf{B}_{ij}.

In tensor network diagrams, the Hadamard product can easily be represented using copy tensors:

Remark 8
.

We list here some useful properties of the Hadamard product.

•

The Hadamard product of a tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
with entries in
\{0,1\}
with itself is
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
. This is in particular true for the copy tensor:

Let
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times d_{3}}
be a 3rd way copy tensor. Then the Hadamard product
\bm{\mathcal{T}}*\bm{\mathcal{T}}
in tensor networks is:

\bm{\mathcal{T}}*\bm{\mathcal{T}}=\hbox to54.33pt{\vbox to72.11pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 30.21486pt\lower-33.20848pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

To conclude this chapter, we introduce several useful results in the next section.

2.3
Some Useful Properties of Tensor Networks

In this section, we list several useful results about tensor networks.

Bounding the Rank of Matricizations.

Any tensor network structure induces a collection of upper bounds on the matricizations of the underlying tensor. More precisely, for an arbitrary tensor network, the rank of a given matricization is bounded by the weight of any cut separating the row legs from the column legs in the graph. Here, the weight of a cut refers to the product of the dimensions of the edges that form the cut. This is formalized in the following theorem.

Theorem 9
.

(Rank of matricization of TN)
Let
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times\dots\times d_{p}}
be given as a tensor network, and let
I\subset[p]
. Then, for any cut
\mathcal{C}
separating the legs corresponding to indices in
I
from the ones in
[p]\setminus I
in the TN,

\mathrm{rank}(\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{(I)})\leq\prod_{e\in\mathrm{cutset}(\mathcal{C})}\mathrm{dim}(e),

where
\mathrm{cutset}(\mathcal{C})
is the cut-set
3
3

3

Formally, the TN is a graph
G=(V,E)
. Each dimension of
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
is associated with one vertex in
V
: the one to which the corresponding dangling leg is attached. Any cut of this graph
\mathcal{C}
is a partition of
V
:
\mathcal{C}=(V_{1},V_{2})
. In the theorem, we consider cuts that separate indices in
I
from the other ones, i.e. such that
I\subseteq V_{1}
(and thus
([p]\setminus I)\subseteq V_{2}
since
(V_{1},V_{2})
is a partition of
V
). The cut-set of
\mathcal{C}
is the set of edges that have one endpoint in
V_{1}
and one in
V_{2}
:
\mathrm{cutset}(\mathcal{C})=\{(u,v)\in E\mid u\in V_{1},v\in V_{2}\}
.
of
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathrm{dim}(e)
is the dimension of the edge
e
in the tensor network.

Let us illustrate this theorem with some examples. First, we can obtain the classical bound on the rank of a product of matrices as a particular case. Let
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times R}
and
\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times n}
. For the matrix (i.e., second-order tensor)
\mathbf{AB}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}
, the theorem gives us the bound

\bm{\mathcal{G}}\in\mathbb{R}^{R_{1}\times\cdots\times R_{4}}
,
\mathbf{A}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{R_{1}\times d_{1}},\mathbf{A}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{R_{2}\times d_{2}},\mathbf{A}_{3}\in\mathbb{R}^{R_{3}\times d_{3}}

\mathbf{A}_{4}\in\mathbb{R}^{R_{4}\times d_{4}}
and consider the tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}=\bm{\mathcal{G}}\times_{1}\mathbf{A}_{1}\times_{2}\mathbf{A}_{2}\times_{3}\mathbf{A}_{3}\times_{4}\mathbf{A}_{4}
. Theorem
9
can be used for example to obtain an upper bound on the rank of the first matricization of
\bm{\mathcal{T}}

TN Edges and Sum Tensors.

Let
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
be a tensor given as a TN. Any edge in which the TN corresponds to one way to express the tensor as a sum of tensors of the same size as
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
. This follows directly from the definition of edges in TNs. An edge represents a contraction, which is a sum. We illustrate this concept with examples. First, consider a rank-
R
factorization of an
m\times n
matrix. The edge in the TN corresponds to expressing the matrix as a sum of
R
(rank-one) matrices:

We recognize here that this TN corresponds to a sum of Kronecker products!

Tensors, Multilinear Maps and Polynomials.

We can think of tensors as
representations of multi-linear maps
, in exactly the same sense that matrices represent linear maps. Recall that a matrix
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}
represents a linear map
\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}
via
\mathbf{x}\mapsto\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}
. In tensor network notation, this is simply

Linearity means that
\mathbf{A}(\alpha\mathbf{x}+\beta\mathbf{z})=\alpha\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}+\beta\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}
for all
\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}
and
\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
. A tensor is the natural generalization when the map is linear
in several arguments separately
. Concretely, an order-
N
tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
defines a map that takes
N
input vectors and returns a scalar by contracting along all modes:

f(\mathbf{x}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{x}^{(N)}):=\langle\bm{\mathcal{T}},\ \mathbf{x}^{(1)}\circ\cdots\circ\mathbf{x}^{(N)}\rangle=\sum_{i_{1}=1}^{d_{1}}\cdots\sum_{i_{N}=1}^{d_{N}}\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{i_{1}\cdots i_{N}}\,\mathbf{x}^{(1)}_{i_{1}}\cdots\mathbf{x}^{(N)}_{i_{N}}.

This map is
multi-linear
: it is linear in each
\mathbf{x}^{(k)}
when the other vectors are fixed. In tensor network diagrams, this is simply

\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}=\bm{\mathcal{T}}\times_{1}\mathbf{x}\times_{2}\mathbf{x}\cdots\times_{N}\mathbf{x}=\sum_{i_{1},\dots,i_{N}}\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{i_{1}\cdots i_{N}}\,\mathbf{x}_{i_{1}}\cdots\mathbf{x}_{i_{N}}\in\mathbb{R}.

is a
homogeneous
multivariate polynomial of degree
N
(every monomial has total degree exactly
N
). The tensor entries are precisely the coefficients of this polynomial in the monomial basis
(\mathbf{x}_{i_{1}}\cdots\mathbf{x}_{i_{N}})_{i_{1},\cdots,i_{N}}
.

If instead we contract an order-
(N+1)
tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times\cdots\times d\times p}
with
N
copies of
\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}
, leaving the last leg free, we obtain a vector-valued homogeneous polynomial map
\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}
:

p(\mathbf{x})=\bm{\mathcal{T}}\times_{1}\mathbf{x}\times_{2}\mathbf{x}\cdots\times_{N}\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}.

Finally,
non-homogeneous
polynomials can be obtained using a simple trick:
append a constant
1
to the input vector
. Let
\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}
and define the augmented vector
\tilde{\mathbf{x}}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}\\
1\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}
. If
\widetilde{\bm{\mathcal{T}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{(d+1)\times\cdots\times(d+1)}
is an order-
N
tensor, then

\tilde{p}(\mathbf{x}):=\widetilde{\bm{\mathcal{T}}}\times_{1}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\times_{2}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\cdots\times_{N}\tilde{\mathbf{x}},

is a polynomial in
\mathbf{x}
of degree at most
N
(some factors can pick the last coordinate, which is the constant
1
, thereby lowering the degree of the corresponding monomials). In other words, a single homogeneous tensor polynomial in the augmented variables
(x_{1},\dots,x_{d},1)
compactly represents a general multivariate polynomial in
(x_{1},\dots,x_{d})
. This viewpoint is especially useful in practice: it lets us treat bias terms and lower-degree interactions using the same contraction machinery as the homogeneous case, simply by adding one extra dimension to each mode and fixing it to
1
.

3
Tensor Decompositions

Working with high-order tensors is computationally expensive because the number of elements grows exponentially with the tensor’s order. Tensor decompositions have emerged as powerful and efficient tools to address this issue.
Similar to matrix factorizations, tensor decompositions break down a high-order tensor into smaller components with lower-order and fewer entries, making computations more tractable. However, the notion of the rank of a matrix can be extended in various ways for tensors, each of them associated with a different factorization/decomposition model.
In this chapter, we introduce the most well-known tensor decomposition models.

3.1
CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) Decomposition

The CP decomposition
[
16
]
of an
N
-th order tensor
\bm{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
decomposes
\bm{\mathcal{A}}
as the sum of a finite number of rank-one tensors. Equivalently, it is a linear combination of
R
rank-one tensors where
R
is called the rank of the decomposition:

\bm{\mathcal{A}}=\sum_{r=1}^{R}\mathbf{a}^{(r)}_{1}\circ\dots\circ\mathbf{a}^{(r)}_{N},

where
\mathbf{a}^{(1)}_{n},\dots,\mathbf{a}^{(R)}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{n}}
for each
n\in[N]
.

By grouping all the vectors
\mathbf{a}^{(r)}_{n}
in factor matrices,

\mathbf{A}_{1}={\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{a}^{(1)}_{1}&\dots&\mathbf{a}^{(R)}_{1}\\
\end{pmatrix}}{\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times R}},\dots,\mathbf{A}_{N}={\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{a}^{(1)}_{N}&\dots&\mathbf{a}^{(R)}_{N}\\
\end{pmatrix}}{\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{N}\times R}},

the CP decomposition is concisely noted as
\bm{\mathcal{A}}=\llbracket\mathbf{A}_{1},\cdots,\mathbf{A}_{N}\rrbracket
.

In tensor networks, a CP decomposition
\bm{\mathcal{A}}=\llbracket\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C}\rrbracket
is represented by

\displaystyle=\sum_{r_{1}=1}^{R}\sum_{r_{2}=1}^{R}\sum_{r_{3}=1}^{R}\delta_{r_{1}r_{2}r_{3}}\mathbf{A}_{ir_{1}}\mathbf{B}_{jr_{2}}\mathbf{C}_{kr_{3}}=\sum_{r=1}^{R}\mathbf{A}_{ir}\mathbf{B}_{jr}\mathbf{C}_{kr}

\displaystyle=\sum_{r=1}^{R}(\mathbf{a}_{r})_{i}(\mathbf{b}_{r})_{j}(\mathbf{c}_{r})_{k}=\sum_{r=1}^{R}(\mathbf{a}_{r}\circ\mathbf{b}_{r}\circ\mathbf{c}_{r})_{ijk}

\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{r=1}^{R}\mathbf{a}_{r}\circ\mathbf{b}_{r}\circ\mathbf{c}_{r}\right)_{ijk}

CP Rank of a Tensor

The most fundamental and oldest concept of the tensor rank is the CP rank, first introduced by
[
16
]
. The CP rank of a tensor is defined as the minimum number of rank-one tensors required to express the tensor as their sum.
4
4

4

Note the subtle difference in our terminology between the rank of a CP decomposition and the CP rank of a tensor: the rank of a CP decomposition is the number of summands in a decomposition of the form
\bm{\mathcal{A}}=\sum_{r=1}^{R}\mathbf{a}^{(r)}_{1}\circ\dots\circ\mathbf{a}^{(r)}_{N}
, whereas the CP rank of a tensor
\bm{\mathcal{A}}
is the smallest
R
for which such a decomposition exists. Consequently, if
\bm{\mathcal{A}}
has a rank-
R
CP decomposition, its CP rank is at most
R
, but could be lower.

Although this definition is similar to that of matrix rank, the properties of tensor rank differ significantly. From a computational point of view, a key difference is that, unlike matrix rank, there is no polynomial-time algorithm to determine a tensor’s CP rank. In fact, computing the rank of a tensor is an NP-hard problem
[
15
]
.
There are several variants of the tensor rank, each associated with a specific tensor decomposition. As we progress through this chapter, we will introduce some of these different types of ranks.

Remark 10
.

We list here some interesting properties of the CP rank and the CP decomposition.

1.

From Theorem
9
and Proposition
2
(item 3), one can show that if a tensor
\bm{\mathcal{A}}
admits a rank-
R
CP decomposition, then all its matricizations have rank upper bounded by
R
:

Proposition 11
.

If
\bm{\mathcal{A}}=\llbracket\mathbf{A}_{1},\cdots,\mathbf{A}_{N}\rrbracket
is a rank-
R
CP decomposition of
\bm{\mathcal{A}}
, then
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{(I)})\leq R
for any
I\subset[N]
.

The following tensor network illustrates this result for the matricization of a fourth-order tensor
\bm{\mathcal{A}}=\llbracket\mathbf{A}_{1},\mathbf{A}_{2},\mathbf{A}_{3},\mathbf{A}_{N}\rrbracket
along its first two modes.

2.

The CP rank of a tensor
\bm{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
can easily be upper bounded as
[
20
]

\mathrm{rank}_{\mathrm{CP}}(\bm{\mathcal{A}})\leq\min_{n\in[N]}\prod_{i\neq n}d_{i}.

3.

For second-order tensors
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}}
, the CP rank corresponds exactly to the classical notion of the rank of a matrix.

4.

The CP decomposition
\bm{\mathcal{A}}=\llbracket\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C}\rrbracket
can be expressed using the Kronecker delta

\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{i,j,k}=\sum_{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}}\delta_{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}}\mathbf{A}_{i,r_{1}}\mathbf{B}_{j,r_{2}}\mathbf{C}_{k,r_{3}},

as well as with mode-
n
products (see
2.2
)

\bm{\mathcal{A}}=\bm{\mathcal{I}}\times_{1}\mathbf{A}\times_{2}\mathbf{B}\times_{3}\mathbf{C}

where
\bm{\mathcal{I}}
is the third-order copy tensor.

5.

The rank of the second-order tensors (matrices), over the fields
\mathbb{R}
and
\mathbb{C}
is the same. However, for higher-order tensors (
N
-th order tensors with
N\geq 3
) the rank can vary depending on the decomposition field
[
22
]
.

6.

The number of parameters of a CP decomposition of an
N
-th order
d
-dimensional tensors (
d_{1}=\dots=d_{N}=d
) is
NdR
instead of
d^{N}
for the full tensor. If
R
is small, the number of parameters can be significantly reduced.

The following proposition shows how the mode-
n
matricization of the CP decomposition of a tensor can be expressed using the Khatri-Rao product.

Proposition 12
.

Let
\bm{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times\dots\times d_{N}}
. If
\bm{\mathcal{A}}=\llbracket\mathbf{A}_{1},\mathbf{A}_{2},\dots,\mathbf{A}_{N}\rrbracket
, then

\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{(n)}=\mathbf{A}_{n}\left(\mathbf{A}_{1}\odot\dots\odot\mathbf{A}_{(n-1)}\odot\mathbf{A}_{(n+1)}\odot\dots\odot\mathbf{A}_{N}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}.

N=3
and
n=1
,

3.2
Tucker Decomposition

The Tucker decomposition
33
factorizes a
N
-th order tensor
into smaller tensor and factor matrices. In this decomposition, the smaller
tensor is called the
core tensor
. The Tucker
decomposition consists of
N
mode-
n
products (see, e.g., Section
2.2
)
between the core tensor and the factor matrices.

Let
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\dots\times d_{N}}
. A Tucker decomposition of
\bm{\mathcal{T}}

is given by

\bm{\mathcal{T}}=\bm{\mathcal{G}}\times_{1}\mathbf{U}_{1}\times_{2}\mathbf{U}_{2}\times_{3}\dots\times_{N}\mathbf{U}_{N},

where
\bm{\mathcal{G}}\in\mathbb{R}^{R_{1}\times\dots\times R_{N}}
is the core tensor and

\mathbf{U}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}\times R_{i}}
for
i\in[N]
are the factor matrices.
The
N
-tuple
(R_{1},\dots,R_{N})
is called the
rank
of Tucker
decomposition.

The Tucker decomposition of a fourth-order tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\cdots\times d_{4}}
can be illustrated using tensor networks notation as follows.

\mathbf{U}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}\times R_{i}}

below).

Multi-linear rank

The
multi-linear (or Tucker) rank
5
5

5

Note the distinction between the rank
(R_{1},\dots,R_{n})
of a Tucker
decomposition
,
given by the size of the core tensor
\bm{\mathcal{G}}
appearing in

\bm{\mathcal{T}}=\bm{\mathcal{G}}\times_{1}\mathbf{U}_{1}\times_{2}\dots\times_{N}\mathbf{U}_{N}
, and the
(Tucker) multi-linear rank of a tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
, which is defined as the
minimal such tuple.
of a tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
is the smallest tuple
(R_{1},\dots,R_{N})

for which there exists a rank-
(R_{1},\dots,R_{N})
decomposition of
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
. Since there is only
a partial order on tuples of integers, one may ask whether this notion of rank is well defined.
The following proposition shows that it is.

Proposition 13
.

Let
\bm{\mathcal{T}}=\bm{\mathcal{G}}\times_{1}\mathbf{U}_{1}\times_{2}\mathbf{U}_{2}\times_{3}\dots\times_{N}\mathbf{U}_{N}
and

\bm{\mathcal{T}}=\tilde{\bm{\mathcal{G}}}\times_{1}\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{1}\times_{2}\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{2}\times_{3}\dots\times_{N}\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{N}
be two
Tucker decompositions of the same tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
of rank-
(R_{1},R_{2},\dots,R_{n})
and

(\tilde{R}_{1},\tilde{R}_{2},\dots,\tilde{R}_{n})
, respectively. Then
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
admits a Tucker decomposition of rank-
(\min(R_{1},\tilde{R}_{1}),\min(R_{2},\tilde{R}_{2}),\dots,\min(R_{N},\tilde{R}_{N}))
.

Proof.

N=3
. Applying the mode-
1
unfolding and Theorem
9
to each of the two Tucker decompositions of
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
we obtain the following:

Computing The Tucker Decomposition.

In contrast with the CP decomposition, which is NP-hard to compute, finding an exact Tucker decomposition (and in particular the one with minimal multi-linear rank) can be achieved in polynomial time by successive SVDs.

The basic idea of the Tucker decomposition algorithm is to find the
R_{n}
leading left singular vectors
in mode-
n
, independently of the other modes. This algorithm, known as
Higher-Order SVD (HOSVD)

[
7
]
, is depicted below. For simplicity, we illustrate this process for
N=4
:

\bm{\mathcal{T}}

d_{1}

d_{3}

d_{2}

d_{4}

\underrightarrow{\text{mode-1 matricization}}

\mathbf{T}

d_{2}

d_{4}

d_{3}

d_{1}

\rightarrow

\mathbf{U}_{1}

\mathbf{\Sigma}_{1}

\mathbf{V}_{1}

d_{3}

R_{1}

d_{1}

R_{1}

d_{2}

d_{4}

Keep
\mathbf{U}_{1}
.

\bm{\mathcal{T}}

d_{1}

d_{3}

d_{2}

d_{4}

\underrightarrow{\text{mode-2 matricization}}

\mathbf{T}

d_{2}

d_{3}

d_{1}

d_{4}

\rightarrow

\mathbf{U}_{2}

\mathbf{\Sigma}_{2}

\mathbf{V}_{2}

d_{3}

R_{2}

d_{2}

R_{2}

d_{1}

d_{4}

Keep
\mathbf{U}_{2}
.

\bm{\mathcal{T}}

d_{1}

d_{3}

d_{2}

d_{4}

\underrightarrow{\text{mode-3 matricization}}

\mathbf{T}

d_{3}

d_{2}

d_{1}

d_{4}

\rightarrow

\mathbf{U}_{3}

\mathbf{\Sigma}_{3}

\mathbf{V}_{3}

d_{2}

R_{3}

d_{3}

R_{3}

d_{1}

d_{4}

Keep
\mathbf{U}_{3}
.

\bm{\mathcal{T}}

d_{1}

d_{3}

d_{2}

d_{4}

\underrightarrow{\text{mode-4 matricization}}

\mathbf{T}

d_{4}

d_{2}

d_{1}

d_{3}

\rightarrow

\mathbf{U}_{4}

\mathbf{\Sigma}_{4}

\mathbf{V}_{4}

d_{2}

R_{4}

d_{4}

R_{4}

d_{1}

d_{3}

Keep
\mathbf{U}_{4}
.

If all the SVD above are exact, i.e.
R_{n}=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{(n)})
for each
n
, then we have that
\bm{\mathcal{T}}\times_{n}\mathbf{U}_{n}\mathbf{U}_{n}^{\mathsf{T}}=\bm{\mathcal{T}}
for all
n
, and thus
\bm{\mathcal{T}}=\bm{\mathcal{T}}\times_{1}\mathbf{U}_{1}\mathbf{U}_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}\times_{2}\cdots\times_{N}\mathbf{U}_{N}\mathbf{U}_{N}^{\mathsf{T}}
. As an example, for
N=4
we have:

\hbox to69.65pt{\vbox to39.4pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip-170.88689pt\lower-23.71666pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}
{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} {}\lxSVG@fillstroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 285.43 0 C 285.43 5.44 281.03 9.84 275.59 9.84 C 270.15 9.84 265.75 5.44 265.75 0 C 265.75 -5.44 270.15 -9.84 275.59 -9.84 C 281.03 -9.84 285.43 -5.44 285.43 0 Z M 275.59 0}{} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

where the tensor
\bm{\mathcal{G}}=\bm{\mathcal{T}}\times_{1}\mathbf{U}_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}\times_{2}\dots\times_{4}\mathbf{U}_{4}^{\mathsf{T}}
.

The core tensor
\bm{\mathcal{G}}\in\mathbb{R}^{R_{1}\times\dots\times R_{4}}
along with the factor matrices
\mathbf{U}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{U}_{4}
forms a Tucker decomposition of the tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
. If all the SVDs of the matricization of
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
are exact, the resulting Tucker decomposition will be exact as well. When using truncated SVDs, the overall approximation error of the Tucker decomposition can be expressed as a function of the errors made in each truncated SVD (see
[
7
]
).

Multi-linear rank and rank of matricizations

The algorithm above shows that, if
\tilde{R}_{n}=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{(n)})
for all
n
, then there exists a Tucker decomposition of rank
(\tilde{R}_{1},\dots,\tilde{R}_{N})
, showing that the multi-linear rank
(R_{1},\dots,R_{N})
of
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
is upper bounded by the rank of the matricizations:
R_{n}\leq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{(n)})
for all
n
. It is also easy to show that the multi-linear rank is lower bounded by the rank of the matricizations. Indeed, suppose
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
has multi-linear rank-
(R_{1},\dots,R_{N})
. Then, there exists a rank-
(R_{1},\dots,R_{N})
Tucker decomposition
\bm{\mathcal{T}}=\bm{\mathcal{G}}\times_{1}\mathbf{U}_{1}\times_{2}\dots\times_{N}\mathbf{U}_{N}
. Using Theorem
9
, we can easily see that this implies
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{(n)})\leq R_{n}
for all
n
.
This proves the following theorem.

Theorem 14
.

The multi-linear rank-
(R_{1},R_{2},\dots,R_{N})
of a tensor
\bm{\mathcal{T}}
is given by the rank of its matricizations, i.e.,
R_{n}=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{\mathcal{T}}_{(n)})
for
n\in[N]
.

Remark 15
.

We list here some interesting properties of the Tucker decomposition and the Higher-Order SVD (HOSVD) algorithm for computing it.

1.

If
\bm{\mathcal{T}}=\bm{\mathcal{G}}\times_{1}\mathbf{U}_{1}\times_{2}\dots\times_{N-1}\mathbf{U}_{N-1}\times_{N}\mathbf{U}_{N}
with all the
\mathbf{U}_{i}
orthogonal, then
\left\lVert\bm{\mathcal{T}}\right\rVert_{F}=\left\lVert\bm{\mathcal{G}}\right\rVert_{F}
and
\mathrm{vec}(\bm{\mathcal{G}})=(\mathbf{U}_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathbf{U}_{N})\mathrm{vec}(\bm{\mathcal{T}})
.
Indeed, for
N=3
we have

\displaystyle(\mathbf{U}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{U}_{2}\otimes\mathbf{U}_{3})\mathrm{vec}(\bm{\mathcal{T}})

Observing that
\mathbf{U}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{U}_{2}\otimes\mathbf{U}_{3}
is a left-orthogonal matrix, it follows that

\left\lVert\bm{\mathcal{T}}\right\rVert=\left\lVert\mathrm{vec}(\bm{\mathcal{T}})\right\rVert=\left\lVert(\mathbf{U}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{U}_{2}\otimes\mathbf{U}_{3})\mathrm{vec}(\bm{\mathcal{T}})\right\rVert=\left\lVert\mathrm{vec}(\bm{\mathcal{G}})\right\rVert=\left\lVert\bm{\mathcal{G}}\right\rVert
.

∎

4.

For an
N
-th order
d
-dimensional tensor, the number of parameters in its Tucker decomposition is
\mathcal{O}(R^{N}+NdR)
assuming
R_{1}=\dots=R_{N}=R
.

5.

We conclude this section by showing how the mode-
n
matricization of the Tucker decomposition of a tensor can be expressed using Kronecker products.

Proposition 16
.

Let
\bm{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times\dots\times d_{N}}
. If
\bm{\mathcal{A}}=\bm{\mathcal{G}}\times_{1}\mathbf{U}_{1}\times_{2}\dots\times_{N}\mathbf{U}_{N}
then

\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{(i)}=\mathbf{U}_{i}\bm{\mathcal{G}}_{(i)}\left(\mathbf{U}_{1}\otimes\dots\otimes\mathbf{U}_{(i-1)}\otimes\mathbf{U}_{(i+1)}\otimes\dots\otimes\mathbf{U}_{N}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}.

Proof.

Assume
N=3
and
n=1
, then we obtain

3.3
Tensor Train (TT) Decomposition

The Tensor Train (TT) decomposition
[
29
]
is another popular tensor factorization model. It decomposes an
N
-th order tensor into
N
smaller third-order tensors.
A rank-
(R_{1},\dots,R_{N-1})

tensor train decomposition
of a tensor
\bm{\mathcal{S}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
factorizes it into a product of
N
third-order tensors
6
6

6

The first and last cores can be though as matrices rather than third-order tensors since they have a singleton dimension. However, considering them as third-rd order tensors allows us to lighten some notations.
,
\bm{\mathcal{G}}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{R_{n-1}\times d_{n}\times R_{n}}
for
n\in[N]
, with
R_{0}=R_{N}=1
:

\bm{\mathcal{S}}_{i_{1},\cdots,i_{N}}=\sum_{r_{0}=1}^{R_{0}}\sum_{r_{1}=1}^{R_{1}}\cdots\sum_{r_{N-1}=1}^{R_{N-1}}\sum_{r_{N}=1}^{R_{N}}\prod_{n=1}^{N}\bm{\mathcal{G}}_{n}(r_{n-1},i_{n},r_{n}):=\TT(({\bm{\mathcal{G}}_{n}})_{n=1}^{N}),

for all
i_{1}\in[d_{1}],\cdots,i_{N}\in[d_{N}]
.
The
TT-rank
of
\bm{\mathcal{S}}
is the smallest

(R_{1},R_{2},\dots,R_{N-1})
such that
\bm{\mathcal{S}}
admits an exact rank-
(R_{1},R_{2},\dots,R_{N-1})
TT-decomposition
\bm{\mathcal{S}}=\TT(({\bm{\mathcal{G}}_{n}})_{n=1}^{N})
.
Similarly to the CP and Tucker decomposition, the rank can be viewed as a hyperparameter that controls the expressivity of the TT decomposition. That is, with a sufficiently large rank, a TT decomposition can represent any arbitrary tensor. The following tensor network illustrates the rank-
(R_{1},R_{2},R_{3})
TT decomposition of a fourth-order tensor:

The TT decomposition was initially introduced in the quantum physics and condensed matter community as
Matrix Product States (MPS)
. In this context, the dimensions of the internal edges are referred to as
bond dimensions
, and the free legs are called
physical dimensions
.
Next, we show how an exact TT decomposition of a tensor
\bm{\mathcal{S}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\dots\times d_{N}}
can be computed in polynomial time using successive singular value decomposition (SVD). This algorithm is known as the TT-SVD algorithm
[
29
]
, but was introduced earlier in the quantum physics community and referred to as
successive Schmidt decompositions

[
35
,
24
]
.
Before presenting the TT-SVD algorithm, we introduce the notions of left and right orthogonality for third-order tensors.

Definition 4
.

A core tensor
\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{R_{n-1}\times d_{n}\times R_{n}}
for
n\in[N]
is left-orthogonal if
(\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n})_{(3)}^{\mathsf{T}}(\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n})_{(3)}=\mathbf{I}_{R_{n}}
and right-orthogonal if
(\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n})_{(1)}(\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n})_{(1)}^{\mathsf{T}}=\mathbf{I}_{R_{n-1}}
. This can be illustrated using tensor networks
as follows:

The following theorem establishes the existence of a minimal tensor train decomposition for any tensor, and its proof is constructive, outlining the TT-SVD algorithm.

Theorem 17
.

(
Computing (Orthogonal) Tensor Train Decomposition.
)
For any
\bm{\mathcal{S}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\dots\times d_{N}}
, let
\bm{\mathcal{S}}_{([n])}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\dots d_{n}\times d_{n+1}\dots d_{N}}
be the matricization obtained by mapping the first
n
modes of
\bm{\mathcal{S}}
to the rows of
\bm{\mathcal{S}}_{[n]}
. Then the TT rank
(R_{1},\cdots,R_{N-1})
of
\bm{\mathcal{S}}
is given
by

R_{n}=\mathrm{rank}~(\bm{\mathcal{S}}_{([n])})
for all
n\in[N-1]
.

Proof.

Let
R_{n}=\mathrm{rank}~(\bm{\mathcal{S}}_{([n])})
. We first show that we can construct a TT decomposition of
\bm{\mathcal{S}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\cdots\times d_{N}}
of rank
(R_{1},R_{2},\cdots,R_{N-1})
by successive QR decomposition. For simplicity, we consider the case
N=4
, but the argument can easily be generalized.

We first take a QR decomposition of the first mode matricization of
\mathbf{\bm{\mathcal{S}}}
, which is of rank-
R_{1}
:

\bm{\mathcal{S}}

d_{1}

d_{3}

d_{2}

d_{4}

\underrightarrow{\text{mode-1 matricization}}

\bm{\mathcal{S}}

d_{2}

d_{4}

d_{3}

d_{1}

\underrightarrow{\text{QR}}

\mathbf{Q}_{1}

\mathbf{R}_{1}

d_{1}

R_{1}

d_{2}

d_{4}

d_{3}

Keep
\mathbf{Q}_{1}
, resume with
\mathbf{R}_{1}
.

Then, we do a QR decomposition of
\mathbf{R}_{1}
obtained at the previous step:

\mathbf{R}_{1}

R_{1}

d_{2}

d_{4}

d_{3}

\underrightarrow{\text{reshape}}

\mathbf{R}_{1}

R_{1}

d_{2}

d_{4}

d_{3}

\underrightarrow{\text{QR}}

\mathbf{Q}_{2}

\mathbf{R}_{2}

d_{2}

R_{1}

R_{2}

d_{4}

d_{3}

Keep
\mathbf{Q}_{2}
, resume with
\mathbf{R}_{2}
.

For the exact QR decomposition to be of rank-
R_{2}
, we first need to show that
the rank of
\mathbf{R}_{1}
, reshaped as a
R_{1}d_{2}\times d_{3}d_{4}
is at most
R_{2}
. Observe that, since
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{\mathcal{S}}_{([2])})=R_{2}
,
there exist
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}d_{2}\times R_{2}}
and

\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{R_{2}\times d_{3}d_{4}}
such that
\bm{\mathcal{S}}_{([2])}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}
, i.e.,

9
, the TN above implies that reshaping
\mathbf{R}_{1}
into a
R_{1}d_{2}\times d_{3}d_{4}

matrix, yields a matrix of rank at most
R_{2}
.
By repeating the steps above for
\mathbf{R}_{2}
, we ultimately obtain a TT decomposition with rank-
(R_{1},R_{2},R_{3})
where
R_{n}=\mathrm{rank}{(\bm{\mathcal{S}}_{([n])})}
for
n\in[3]
, i.e.,

(12)

resulting in a TT decomposition where all cores are orthogonal except for the last core.

The algorithm above shows that, if
\tilde{R}_{n}=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{\mathcal{S}}_{([n])})
for all
n
, then there exists a TT decomposition of rank-
(\tilde{R}_{1},\dots,\tilde{R}_{N-1})
, showing that the TT rank
(R_{1},\dots,R_{N-1})
of
\bm{\mathcal{S}}
is upper-bounded by the rank of the matricizations:
R_{n}\leq\mathrm{rank}(\bm{\mathcal{S}}_{([n])})
for all
n
. It is also easy to show that the TT rank is lower-bounded by the rank of the matricizations. Indeed, suppose that
\bm{\mathcal{S}}
has the TT rank
(R_{1},\dots,R_{N-1})
. Then, there exists a rank-
(R_{1},\dots,R_{N-1})
TT decomposition. Using Theorem
9
, we can easily see that this implies
\mathrm{rank}(\bm{\mathcal{S}}_{([n])})\leq R_{n}
for all
n
.
∎

Although the proof above uses successive QR decompositions to construct an exact TT decomposition, the algorithm commonly referred to as TT-SVD uses SVDs of the successive unfoldings. In the exact case, retaining all nonzero singular values yields TT ranks

R_{n}=\mathrm{rank}(\bm{\mathcal{S}}_{([n])})
.
The advantage of the SVD formulation is that it immediately provides a low-rank approximation algorithm: at each step, truncated SVD can be used to prescribed TT ranks or according to a tolerance on the discarded singular values
[
29
,
17
]
.

Another widely used approach for decomposing a tensor into the tensor-train (TT) format is the Alternating Least Squares (ALS) algorithm. Before introducing this method, we first describe the canonical form of the TT decomposition.

Definition 5
.

The TT decomposition
\TT(({\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n}})_{n=1}^{N})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times\dots\times d_{N}}
is said to be in canonical form with respect to a fixed index
j\in[N]
if all cores with
n<j
are left-orthogonal and all cores with
n>j
are right-orthogonal, e.g., the following TT decomposition is in canonical form with respect to its third core tensor:

The cores on the left side of
\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{3}
are left-orthogonal and the cores on the right are right-orthogonal. The core
\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{3}
is called the center of orthogonality. Note that any TT decomposition can be efficiently converted to a canonical form w.r.t. any index
j\in[N]
by performing a series of QR decompositions on the core tensors
[
18
,
8
]
.

Computing TT with Alternating Least Squares (ALS)

The single-site Tensor Train Alternating Least Squares (TT-ALS) method
[
18
]
starts with a TT decomposition in canonical form, initialized with a crude approximation (e.g., with random cores, or using TT-SVD).
In the first step, the core

\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{1}
of the decomposition is non-orthogonal. During sweeps from left to right (respectively, right to left), the algorithm keeps all cores fixed except for the
n
-th one,
\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n}
, and optimizes it to minimize the distance to the target tensor. The resulting minimization problem is a simple least-squares problem, hence the name ALS.
After updating
\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n}
, a QR decomposition is applied to ensure numerical stability and to maintain the canonical form. The non-orthonormal factor is then merged into the left (or right, depending on the sweep direction), a step known as
core orthogonalization
.
